Where it began

Saeed Anwar was born in Karachi on 6 September 1968. As a boy he moved with his family to Canada, spending a few years there before they came home to Karachi in 1977. He studied computer system engineering at the NED University of Engineering and Technology, graduating in 1989, and had thought of a master's degree in the United States.

The game got there first. He played his first one-day international in January 1989, under Imran Khan, at the WACA. A Test cap followed against the West Indies at Faisalabad in 1990.

The player

That first Test was not kind to him. Curtly Ambrose and Ian Bishop sent him back without a run in either innings. He took it in his stride. In his third Test, in February 1994, he made 169 against New Zealand.

He played 55 Tests between 1990 and 2001 and scored 4,052 runs at 45.53, with 11 hundreds and 25 fifties. His best was 188 not out at Eden Gardens in the Asian Test Championship of 1998–99, when he carried his bat through the innings, only the third Pakistani to do so. In one-day cricket his 194 against India at Chennai in 1997 was, at the time, the highest score anyone had made in a men's one-day international, and when he retired in 2003 no Pakistani had made more one-day hundreds than his 20.

What made him special

Timing was his gift. He never seemed to swing hard, yet the ball raced away, most often through the off side, and his flick off the pads turned up in almost every innings. Few batsmen of the 1990s were easier on the eye.

He was at his best where batsmen from Asia often found life hard. Against Australia his Test average was 59.06, the highest by any Pakistani, and he once made hundreds against them in back-to-back Tests. In England in 1996 he scored 362 runs at 60.33, and his 118 at Kingsmead in 1997–98 helped Pakistan to their first Test win in South Africa. With the ball he was less of a threat: he bowled a little left-arm spin in Tests, but a wicket never came his way.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1997, and Pakistan awarded him the Pride of Performance in 2000. He played in three World Cups, in 1996, 1999 and 2003, and was Pakistan's leading run-scorer at each of them. In 1999 his hundreds against Zimbabwe and then New Zealand, in the semi-final, helped carry the side to the final. He also captained Pakistan in seven Tests and 11 one-day internationals. He left the game in 2003 with a second trade, as a computer engineer.

And finally

Sharjah suited him. He made seven one-day hundreds there, three of them in a row in 1993–94. With Aamir Sohail he opened in 32 one-day innings in a row, more than any Pakistan opening pair before them. For a man who began his Test career with two noughts, he made up the numbers handsomely.
